description: I am an Electrical and Electronics Engineering student at New Horizon College of Engineering, Bangalore, with interests in software development, AI and emerging technologies. I have experience building full-stack applications and AI-powered solutions, and serve as a Google Student Ambassador. I enjoy interdisciplinary problem-solving, collaborative engineering and exploring technology-driven solutions to real-world challenges.

AURORA: The Last Ascent is a cooperative Roblox game for 1-4 players that teaches the trade-offs of real mission design. A crew crash-lands on a fictional, Mars-like planet and has one goal: reach orbit.

Each player takes a role (Commander, Pilot, Mechanic or Science Officer). Together they scavenge resources, repair power, communications and propulsion, and make propellant through a multi-step process modelled on real in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) chemistry. In the Mission Planner, they choose payload, propellant load and target orbit. The planner shows live pass/marginal/fail checks for mass, thrust-to-weight, power and delta-v. Then the Pilot flies the rocket to orbit using a custom flight simulation (gravity, a NASA-based Mars atmosphere model, drag and the rocket equation), not Roblox’s built-in physics.

The debrief shows exactly how much delta-v gravity, drag and steering cost, and explains why the mission succeeded or failed. A built-in Codex and short quizzes teach rocket science, ISRU, power and teamwork, and simplified values are clearly labelled. Players learn that every kilogram, watt and decision matters.
details:
What it does
AURORA: The Last Ascent is a cooperative Roblox game for 1-4 players that turns end-to-end mission design into gameplay. A crew crash-lands on a fictional, Mars-like planet. Each player takes a role: Commander, Pilot, Field Mechanic or Science Officer. Together they restore power and oxygen, scan and collect resources, avoid or study unexplained anomalies, and repair propulsion, communications and power. They make propellant through a multi-step process based on real in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) chemistry: ice, water, electrolysis, then methane and oxygen. Nothing is instant.

In the Mission Planner, the team chooses the target orbit, payload (instruments, samples, spares) and propellant load. Live pass/marginal/fail checks cover mass, thrust-to-weight, delta-v, power and oxygen, with a one-line reason and a suggested fix. After a Go/No-Go vote, the Pilot flies the ascent live. The debrief scores the mission and shows how much delta-v gravity, drag and steering cost.

How it works
Roblox’s built-in physics can’t model orbital flight, so the rocket is driven by a custom double-precision flight simulation written in Luau. It uses Mars-analogue gravity, a NASA-based Mars atmosphere model, Mach-dependent drag and engine mass flow. It is checked against the rocket equation, Kepler orbits and energy conservation. The server owns all game state. Clients only send requests, which keeps four-player sessions in sync.

Benefits and intended impact
Players learn by making trade-offs, not by reading. Adding cargo visibly shrinks delta-v, and dust storms cut solar power. Short “Why?” pop-ups, a Codex and a quiz explain each concept at the moment it matters. Verified NASA figures are separated from simplified game values, which carry a gear icon. We want players to leave understanding why mission design is hard, and why teamwork and margins matter.

Tools

  • Roblox Studio and Luau
  • Rojo for syncing code files
  • AI coding assistants (Google Antigravity and Claude) for development
  • NASA public data and studies: Mars Fact Sheet, Glenn Mars atmosphere model, MOXIE results, Mars Ascent Vehicle studies
  • Standard laptops, no special hardware

Creativity
The game is built around survival, but the real lesson is the engineering trade-offs. Aliens are anomalies to study or avoid, so the focus stays on science, not combat. The debrief explains failures using the player’s own flight data.

Factors we considered

  • A 48-hour scope: one complete, playable mission
  • Accuracy versus fun: assisted flight controls for new players
  • Honesty: simplifications are labelled
  • Teamwork: each repair and the launch need several roles
  • Accessibility: solo play, with automation covering absent roles
